questions.q: In JavaScript, what does stock = stock - 3 mean?
questions.explain: In code, = is assignment, and it works right to left. Mathematical equality is written === and produces a boolean.
options: A false equation, because no number equals itself minus 3
Compute stock - 3, then store the result in stock

questions.q: A customer has ₦20,000 and each item costs ₦3,000. Which expression gives the number of items they can afford?
questions.explain: 20,000 / 3,000 is 6.67. You cannot buy part of an item, and 7 would cost ₦21,000, so round down: 6. Math.round would give 7 here.

questions.q: A warehouse packs 50 phones into boxes of 12. Which expression gives the number of boxes needed to pack them all?
questions.explain: 50 / 12 is 4.17. Four boxes hold only 48 phones, so you need 5. "How many do I need to hold everything?" rounds up.

questions.q: Which question does n % 2 === 0 answer?
questions.explain: % gives the remainder of a division. An even number leaves remainder 0 when divided by 2.

questions.q: What makes a JavaScript function behave like a mathematical function?
questions.explain: A mathematical function gives exactly one output for each input. A JavaScript function that reads only its parameters and changes nothing outside (a pure function) behaves the same way.
options: It gives the same output for the same input every time and depends only on its inputs

questions.q: Delivery costs ₦2,000 under ₦10,000, ₦1,000 up to ₦50,000, and nothing above. Which order totals test this rule best?
questions.explain: A piecewise function changes at its boundaries, so bugs hide there. Test on each side of each boundary. The first option only checks the middle of each piece.

questions.q: A price including 7.5% VAT is ₦21,500. Which formula gives the price before VAT?
questions.explain: net × 1.075 = 21,500, so net = 21,500 ÷ 1.075 = 20,000. Subtracting 7.5% of the gross takes VAT on the VAT and gives 19,887.50, which is wrong.

questions.q: You wrote netFromGross(gross). What is the simplest test that it solved the equation correctly?
questions.explain: Substitution: put the answer back into the original equation. If net × 1.075 does not give the gross, the formula is wrong.
options: Check that the result is smaller than the input
Multiply the result by 1.075 and check you get the gross back
Check that the result is a whole number

questions.q: Bola saves ₦12,000 a month. She needs at least ₦50,000. After how many whole months does she have enough?
questions.explain: 12,000 × m ≥ 50,000 gives m ≥ 4.17. Months are whole, so round up: after 4 months she has only ₦48,000; after 5 she has ₦60,000.

questions.q: Two partners share ₦50,000 profit in the ratio 2 : 3. How much does the first partner get?
questions.explain: 2 + 3 = 5 parts, and the first gets 2 of them: 50,000 × 2/5 = 20,000.

questions.q: Oil costs ₦3,000 for 1 litre or ₦5,500 for 2 litres. How should a program decide which is cheaper?
questions.explain: Different quantities must be compared through a ratio: the unit price. The 2-litre bottle is ₦2,750 per litre.
options: Compare the prices per litre: 3,000 and 2,750

questions.q: What is 15% of ₦12,000?
questions.explain: 15% is 15/100, so 12,000 × 15 / 100 = 1,800. ₦10,200 is the price after a 15% discount.

questions.q: A dress gets 20% off, then another 10% off the sale price. How much off the original price is that in total?
questions.explain: The multipliers multiply: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so the customer pays 72% and saves 28%. The second discount applies to the already reduced price.

questions.q: A price of ₦10,000 goes up 25%, then down 25%. What is the final price?
questions.explain: 10,000 × 1.25 = 12,500, then 12,500 × 0.75 = 9,375. The cut is 25% of the higher price, so it removes more than the rise added.

questions.q: A loan rate rises from 10% to 15%. Which statement is correct?
questions.explain: The difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points (15 − 10 = 5). Relative to the old rate, 5 is 50% of 10.
options: It rose by 5 percentage points, which is a 50% increase in the rate

questions.q: ₦300,000 is saved at 8% simple interest a year. How much interest after 2 years?
questions.explain: Simple interest = principal × rate × years = 300,000 × 0.08 × 2 = 48,000. ₦49,920 would be compound interest, where the second year's interest is also paid on the first year's interest.

questions.q: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3 in JavaScript?
questions.explain: Floating point stores the nearest binary value. The tiny errors in 0.1 and 0.2 add up to a visible difference. Almost every language behaves the same.
options: JavaScript has a bug in its addition
Numbers are stored in binary, where 0.1 has no exact form, like 1/3 in decimal
Because 0.3 is too small to store

questions.q: Which calculations with JavaScript numbers are always exact?
questions.explain: Every whole number up to about 9 quadrillion is stored exactly, so whole-number arithmetic in that range is exact. That is why money is stored in kobo.
options: Adding, subtracting and multiplying whole numbers up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER

questions.q: A developer "fixes" floating-point money bugs by calling toFixed(2) before showing totals. What problem remains?
questions.explain: toFixed returns a string for display. The till showed ₦2,700.99 while >= compared against 2700.9900000000002.
options: The number used in comparisons and later sums still carries the error; only the display is rounded

questions.q: How should the price ₦1,999.99 be stored?
questions.explain: Whole kobo keep every addition and subtraction exact. Convert to naira only when showing the amount.

questions.q: Why does the lesson store the VAT rate 7.5% as 750 basis points?
questions.explain: 0.075 is a binary approximation. Multiplying whole kobo by the whole number 750 is exact; the single division and Math.round at the end form the one deliberate rounding step.
options: So the calculation amount * 750 / 10000 multiplies whole numbers and divides only once, just before rounding
Because VAT must be larger than the price

questions.q: Rounding VAT per invoice line gives 552 kobo; rounding once on the total gives 551. What should the developer do?
questions.explain: Both are valid rounding rules; which one applies is a business or legal decision. Consistency matters most: one function everywhere, and receipts that add up.
options: Round both ways and average them
Ask which rule the business or tax authority requires, implement it in one function, and make the printed lines add up to the printed total

questions.q: ₦100 is split three ways as ₦33.33 each. What went wrong?
questions.explain: Rounding each part separately does not preserve the total. Give everyone the rounded-down share in kobo, then hand out the leftover kobo one at a time.
options: The shares add up to ₦99.99; one kobo was lost by rounding each share separately
The shares add up to more than ₦100

questions.q: The invoice function refuses priceKobo: 250.3. Why is that the right behaviour?
questions.explain: Mixing naira and kobo is the most common money bug. Kobo are whole, so a guard with Number.isInteger catches the mix-up at the door instead of charging ₦2.50 for bread.
options: Because a fractional value in a kobo field almost certainly means someone passed naira by mistake

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Multiplication comes before addition, so the first is 3,000 + 500. Parentheses force the addition first in the second.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 40 / 12 = 3.33: 3 full crates, 4 crates to hold everything, and 40 − 36 = 4 bottles left over.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Decimal fractions like 0.1 are approximations in binary; whole numbers are exact. This is why money is stored as whole kobo.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The sum is 2700.9900000000002, which is slightly more than 2700.99, so total >= 2700.99 is true. The problem in the lesson was the other direction: paid >= total, where the customer's exact payment is slightly less than the total.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Adding whole numbers is exact, so the total is exactly 270,099 kobo. Dividing by 100 happens only to display it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 15% of 20,000 is 3,000; the price after a 15% discount is 85% of 20,000, which is 17,000.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Exact VAT on 1,250 kobo is 93.75, which rounds to 94. Three lines rounded separately give 282; rounding the total VAT of 281.25 gives 281.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1,000 / 3 is 333 with 1 left over, and the first person gets the extra kobo. 1,000 / 4 divides exactly, so nobody gets extra.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.round goes to the nearest whole number with halves going up; Math.floor always goes down; Math.ceil always goes up.

questions.q: Write canAfford(budget, price) returning how many whole items fit in the budget, and crates(items, perCrate) returning how many crates are needed to hold all items.
questions.explain: Affording rounds down, holding everything rounds up. When the division is exact (48 / 12), both give the same answer.

questions.q: Write vatKobo(amountKobo, basisPoints) that returns the VAT in whole kobo, rounded to the nearest kobo. 7.5% is 750 basis points.
questions.explain: One basis point is 1/10,000. Multiply first (whole numbers, exact), divide once, and round once. 2,450 × 750 / 10,000 = 183.75, which rounds to 184.

questions.q: Write splitKobo(totalKobo, people) that returns an array of whole-kobo shares that add up exactly to the total, with the leftover kobo going one each to the first people.
questions.explain: Everyone gets the rounded-down share; the remainder is always smaller than the number of people, so handing out one extra kobo each to the first few uses it up exactly.

questions.q: Shelf prices include 7.5% VAT. Write splitGross(grossKobo) that returns { net, vat } in whole kobo, with net + vat exactly equal to the gross. Round only the net.
questions.explain: net × 1.075 = gross, so net = gross ÷ 1.075 = gross × 10,000 / 10,750. Computing the VAT as the difference guarantees the two parts add back to the shelf price.

questions.q: Use a while loop to find after how many whole months savings of ₦12,000 a month first reach at least ₦50,000. Print 5 months style output.
questions.explain: The loop runs while the goal is not met: saved < target is the negation of saved >= target. It matches the formula Math.ceil(50000 / 12000).

questions.q: Write afterDiscounts(price, first, second) that applies a first% discount and then a second% discount on the reduced price. Use whole-number arithmetic: multiply by (100 - p) and divide by 100.
questions.explain: The discounts multiply: 20% then 10% leaves 80% × 90% = 72% of the price, so 28% off in total, not 30%.
